title: Demonstrations For Marijuana Reform In Mexico City. Viva Mexico!

content_html_sanitized:
Saturday was the beginning of a popular holiday weekend in Mexico, Cinco de Mayo, and as good a day as any to demonstrate in favor of the stalled effort to legalize cannabis in our Southern neighbor.

See Advocates Rally In Mexico City To Demand Cannabis Reform

AndThousands of protesters gathered in Mexico City over the weekend, calling on lawmakers to legalize marijuana and end criminal penalties for personal use and cultivation.

 

Oddly, Mexico banned cannabis in 1920, ahead of many countries, and in 1927, cultivation, production, and sale were prohibited. These laws paralleled growing international pressure, especially from the U.S., which pushed prohibition across the Americas.

 

William Randolph Hearst, the newspaper publisher, was a major advocate of reefer madness.

See Marijuana Prohibition Was a Farce from the Beginning

Rethinking the federal war on marijuana is long overdue.  

 

In the 1940s, influential Mexican physician, Dr. Leopoldo Salazar Viniegra argued for medical, scientific, and non-punitive approaches, but U.S. influence suppressed these views. It is sad to think how modern Mexican history would have been so different, if Mexico had listened to the good doctor, instead of American propagandists.

Consequently, from the 1970s onward, Mexico became a major battleground in the U.S.-led War on Drugs. Harsh enforcement targeted cannabis, poppies, and cocaine trafficking. The focus was punitive, with military and police crackdowns, resulting in extreme violence, especially in the border areas.

From 2001, How Marijuana Prohibition Really Works on the Texas/Mexico Border. Contrast with the Situation at the Canadian Border. Great Journalism. And from 2003, see Now, How the Narks Created Smack in Mexico. Replacing Marijuana With Poppies. The Iron Law of Prohibition Keeps Working, But Journalism Does Not.

Finally, in 2000, Mexico decriminalized possession of small amounts (5 grams) of marijuana for personal use. This was meant to focus resources on organized crime. Then in 2015, Mexico’s Supreme Court ruled in favor of personal cultivation for individuals, citing the constitutional right to free development of personality, and in 2017, a federal law legalized medical marijuana, allowing products with less than 1% THC. Placebo?


In 2018, The Mexican Supreme Court ruled that the absolute prohibition of recreational marijuana was unconstitutional, calling on lawmakers to create a regulatory framework.

But Congress delayed passing a legalization bill multiple times, despite extensions from the court. Sounds familiar. See State Efforts to Restrict Voter-Driven Marijuana Reforms (2023–2025). So Whom Do Our Representatives Really Represent?

Finally, in June of 2021, the Supreme Court struck down laws prohibiting personal use and cultivation, effectively decriminalizing adult use, but without full regulation.

As of this year, personal possession and home cultivation of cannabis (within limits) are decriminalized, but there is still no formal regulatory system for commercial production or sales. Even though medical marijuana is legal, access is still limited.

Recreational cannabis is effectively legal for adults, but still lacks clear, nationwide commercial rules, Mexico continues to face legal ambiguity and political delays, leaving a partially reformed system without full implementation. By the way, the Spanish word for “loophole” is escapatoria.  

And now for a special treat, if you haven’t seen it before. Judy Garland in 1935, singing “La Cucaracha”!
